subject: Career
title: Anchoring Your Salary Expectation
description: Learn Anchoring Your Salary Expectation in one minute.

hook.text: The first number spoken in a salary discussion becomes the anchor. Everything revolves around it.

buildup.text: Anchoring bias means the initial figure disproportionately influences the final outcome.

discovery.text: If they anchor low, you're negotiating up from their number. If you anchor first, they adjust to yours.

twist.text: But anchoring too high can end the conversation. The anchor must be aggressive yet defensible.

climax.text: Research shows the party who names a number first usually gets a better outcome.

punchline.text: Whoever sets the anchor controls the range.

quiz.question: Why is the first salary number important?
options: It anchors the entire negotiation range

details.summary: Anchoring is a cognitive bias where the first number mentioned in a negotiation sets the reference point for all subsequent discussion. In interviews, whoever names a salary figure first anchors the range and gains a strategic advantage.
details.whyItMatters: Failing to anchor strategically often leaves thousands of dollars on the table. Understanding this bias lets you control the negotiation frame rather than being controlled by it.
takeaways: The first number spoken becomes the psychological anchor point
Research market rates thoroughly before naming any figure
When possible, let the employer state the range first

faq.question: Should you always let the employer name the salary range first?
faq.answer: Generally yes, because their range reveals the budget ceiling. However, if you have strong market data showing you deserve a premium, naming a well-researched high anchor first can set expectations above their default range.

faq.question: What if the interviewer insists you share your salary expectations first?
faq.answer: Respond with a range based on thorough research rather than a single number. Saying 'based on my research, roles like this typically pay between X and Y' anchors the conversation without locking you into one figure.
